passages.title: Province Targets Holiday Drownings as Schools Close for Summer
paragraphs: Hundreds of children in a province in north-eastern Thailand are spending the school holiday in the water, thanks to a free programme aimed at cutting one of the most common causes of death among the young.

The programme, run by the provincial health office and local schools, offers ten one-hour lessons to children aged six to twelve. Rather than teaching competitive strokes, instructors focus on “survival swimming”: floating on the back, moving a short distance to safety and staying calm.

Children also learn a simple rule for helping others: “shout, throw, don't go.” Instead of jumping in to save a friend, which often results in two deaths rather than one, they call an adult and throw something that floats, such as an empty bottle.

According to the provincial health office, 41 children in the province drowned in 2022. Most died not in swimming pools but in ponds, canals and reservoirs near their homes, and nearly half died during the March-to-May holidays, when many children are left without adult supervision.

Ms. Wanida Srisuk, a teacher and one of the organisers, said many parents in farming villages cannot swim. “They are afraid of the water, so they keep their children away from it, but that does not make the children safer,” she said.

Organisers hope to train 3,000 children by the end of next year, but admit that lessons alone are not enough. They are urging village leaders to put up fences and warning signs around the most dangerous ponds.

questions.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Most children who drown in the province lose their lives in public swimming pools.
Free lessons are teaching children skills that could save them in the water.
Parents in farming villages are being trained to rescue children from ponds.
Village leaders have built fences around the province's most dangerous ponds.

passages.title: Northern City Reviews Six-Month Trial at Busy Junctions
paragraphs: Traffic lights controlled by artificial intelligence have shortened waiting times at some of the busiest junctions in a city in northern Thailand, according to a review of a six-month pilot scheme released this week.

Under the scheme, cameras mounted above twelve intersections count the cars, motorcycles and pedestrians approaching from each direction. Software then adjusts the length of each green light every few seconds. Previously, the lights followed fixed timings that had been set years earlier and were rarely updated.

According to the city's transport department, the average time vehicles spent waiting at the twelve junctions fell by 23 percent during the morning rush hour. Emergency services have also benefited: when an ambulance approaches, the system can detect it and switch the lights ahead to green.

“In the past, police officers often had to stand in the middle of the road and direct traffic by hand,” said Mr. Kittipong Saenkham, an engineer on the project. “Now the lights respond to what is actually happening on the street.”

Not everyone is convinced. Some residents have asked what happens to the video recorded by the cameras and who is allowed to see it. City officials insist that the software keeps only the number of vehicles and that all footage is deleted automatically within 24 hours. Privacy campaigners argue that such promises should be written into law.

Others doubt that the improvements will last. Transport researchers warn that when traffic moves more smoothly, more people may choose to drive, which could eventually bring congestion back to its previous level.
The city will decide early next year whether to extend the system to a further 40 junctions at an estimated cost of 60 million baht.

passages.title: Who Will Teach the Village Children?
paragraphs: At a small primary school in the hills of northern Thailand, Mr. Somchai Phonsawat teaches mathematics, science and physical education, and on Friday afternoons he also runs the school library. With six grades but only four teachers, the school expects everyone to cover several subjects. His situation is common: across rural Thailand, as in many countries, small schools struggle to attract and keep teachers.

The causes are well known. Young graduates tend to prefer towns, where housing is better and further study is easier to arrange. Those who do accept rural posts often apply for a transfer as soon as they are allowed to.

The effects fall hardest on pupils. When a teacher leaves mid-year, classes may be combined or taught by unqualified temporary staff. A 2022 survey of 300 rural schools in the north-east found that nearly one in three had at least one class without a permanent teacher for more than a term. Such disruption has been linked to lower reading scores.

Governments have tried several incentives. Some offer extra allowances for remote postings; others provide free housing or repay the student loans of teachers who stay five years or more. A newer approach is to recruit young people from rural communities, train them and send them back to their home districts, on the assumption that teachers with local roots are more likely to stay.

Early results are encouraging. In one programme, about 80 percent of locally recruited teachers were still in their first school after five years, compared with around half of those hired through the usual system. Yet money alone rarely solves the problem. Teachers interviewed for this article said that what they valued most was support: a head teacher who listened, colleagues to share ideas with and the chance to keep learning.
For Mr. Somchai, who grew up two villages away, leaving has never been an option. “If I go, who will teach these children?” he asks.

questions.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Rural pupils' reading scores are lower than those of children in towns.
Paying teachers more money is the most effective way to keep them in rural schools.
Rural schools struggle to keep teachers, and incentives have only partly helped.
Teachers who grew up in villages are unwilling to work in city schools.

passages.title: Roots Against the Tide
paragraphs: For decades, Thailand's coastal mangrove forests were treated as wasteland. Large areas were cleared for shrimp farms, charcoal production and tourist resorts. Today attitudes have changed, and villagers, scientists and officials are working together to bring the forests back.

The most obvious reason is protection. The dense, tangled roots of mangrove trees slow down waves and trap mud, reducing coastal erosion and, in some cases, storm damage. After the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, several studies reported that villages behind healthy mangrove belts tended to suffer less than those on exposed shores, although scientists caution that no forest can stop the largest waves.

Mangroves are also remarkably good at storing carbon. Because the waterlogged soil beneath them contains little oxygen, dead leaves and roots decay very slowly, and carbon can remain locked in the mud for centuries. A hectare of mangrove may hold several times more carbon than a hectare of tropical forest on land. When the trees are cleared, much of this carbon escapes into the atmosphere.

A third benefit is less visible but matters greatly to coastal families. The shallow, sheltered water among the roots serves as a nursery for young fish, crabs and shrimp. Fishers in restored areas often report larger catches within a few years, although such claims are difficult to verify.

Restoration, however, is harder than it looks. Many early projects simply planted thousands of seedlings on open mudflats, where most of them were washed away or drowned by the tide. Experts now argue that the first step should be to restore the natural flow of water, for example by breaking down the walls of abandoned shrimp ponds, and then allow seeds from nearby trees to settle naturally.

Local involvement appears to be just as important. In one village in southern Thailand, residents have formed a committee that sets rules for cutting wood and organises patrols. “We used to think the forest belonged to no one,” said Mr. Preecha Thongdee, the committee's chairman. “Now we understand that it belongs to all of us.”

In my view, such community-led efforts offer the best hope for Thailand's coasts. Planting seedlings for a photograph is easy; keeping a forest alive for decades requires the commitment of the people who depend on it.

questions.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Most of Thailand's mangroves were cleared to make room for shrimp farms.
Mangroves are valuable, but restoring them needs care and local support.
Mangrove forests can protect coastal villages from even the largest waves.
Fishers catch more fish after planting mangrove seedlings on mudflats.

to show that mangroves can stop any wave

deny
prove

Seawater carries the carbon deep under the ground.

confirm
explain
repeat
questions.explain: ¶4: “although such claims are difficult to verify” หมายถึงคำกล่าวของชาวประมงว่าจับปลาได้มากขึ้นนั้น 'ยืนยัน/ตรวจสอบ' ได้ยาก จึงตรงกับ confirm ตัวเลือก A (increase) เป็นกับดักเพราะประโยคก่อนหน้าพูดถึง larger catches

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT mentioned as a benefit of mangrove forests?

options: Community efforts offer the best hope for the coast.

passages.title: Health Literacy in Clinical Practice: Evidence and Implications
paragraphs: When a doctor prescribes a new medicine, the consultation is usually regarded as complete once the prescription has been written. Yet the success of treatment depends heavily on what happens afterwards: whether the patient understands the instructions, remembers them and is able to act on them at home. The skills involved in this process are collectively known as health literacy. Broadly defined, the term refers to a person's capacity to find, understand, evaluate and use health information in order to make decisions about his or her own care. It therefore goes well beyond the ability to read. It also includes numeracy, the confidence to ask questions and the ability to navigate complex health systems, from booking appointments to understanding insurance forms.

Limited health literacy is far more common than most clinicians assume. Surveys in several countries have suggested that between a third and a half of adults have difficulty with everyday health tasks, such as working out the correct dose of a medicine for a child or interpreting the nutrition label on a packet of food. Older adults, people with long-term illnesses and those with fewer years of schooling are at particular risk. Health literacy, however, is not simply a matter of education. A university professor who has just received a frightening diagnosis may be unable to absorb information that he would normally understand with ease, because anxiety, pain and unfamiliar terminology all reduce comprehension.

The consequences of low health literacy are well documented. Compared with patients who have adequate skills, those with limited health literacy are less likely to take medicines as prescribed and less likely to attend screening programmes. They are admitted to hospital more often, make greater use of emergency services and, among older people, have higher death rates. Some of these associations may partly reflect poverty and the other disadvantages that frequently accompany low literacy. Even after such factors are taken into account, however, a link generally remains.

One reason the problem persists is that it is largely invisible. Patients who struggle with written information often develop strategies to conceal their difficulty: they may claim to have forgotten their glasses, ask to take forms home, or simply nod when a doctor asks whether everything is clear. Shame plays an important part. In a study at a regional hospital in north-eastern Thailand, researchers interviewed 150 patients with type 2 diabetes and found that more than 40 percent could not correctly explain how to take their main medicine, although nearly all of them had told their doctor that the instructions were easy to follow.

Because clinicians cannot reliably identify patients with low health literacy, experts increasingly recommend a “universal precautions” approach: communicating with every patient as though he or she might have difficulty understanding. The best-known technique of this kind is teach-back. At the end of an explanation, the clinician asks the patient to describe, in his or her own words, what has been agreed — for example, “I want to be sure I explained this clearly. Can you tell me how you will take this tablet?” If the answer is incomplete, the clinician explains the point again in a different way and checks once more. Crucially, the method is presented as a test of the clinician's explanation rather than of the patient's intelligence, which reduces embarrassment.

A second strategy is the use of plain language in both speech and writing. This involves replacing medical jargon with everyday words, such as “high blood pressure” instead of “hypertension”, keeping sentences short, and limiting each consultation to a small number of key messages. Written materials can be improved through larger print, generous white space and simple pictures. Such changes may appear minor, yet trials have shown that redesigned medicine labels and leaflets can noticeably improve how accurately patients follow instructions.

Some clinicians object that these techniques take time that busy clinics simply do not have. The available evidence suggests that the additional time is usually modest, often only a minute or two per consultation, and that it may be recovered later through fewer telephone calls, repeat visits and avoidable admissions. Others worry that simplified language may seem patronising to well-educated patients. In practice, few patients complain about information that is easy to understand; clarity tends to be appreciated by everyone, including doctors themselves when they become patients.

Health literacy, then, should not be regarded as a deficit that belongs only to patients. It is equally a property of health systems, which can be designed to be more or less understandable. Yet training in clear communication remains a minor part of many medical and nursing curricula. Making it a core clinical skill, alongside diagnosis and treatment, may be one of the least expensive ways of improving patient outcomes.

options: Many patients misunderstand health information, but better communication can help.
Patients with little schooling should be given simplified leaflets about their medicines.
Doctors in Thailand lack the time to explain medicines properly to their patients.
Health literacy depends mainly on how many years a person has spent in school.

passages.title: Automation and the Future of Work: Evidence, Uncertainty and Policy
paragraphs: Few economic questions provoke as much anxiety as the effect of automation on employment. Each new wave of technology, from the mechanical loom to the industrial robot, has been accompanied by warnings that machines would leave large numbers of people permanently without work. The recent arrival of artificial intelligence systems that can write text, analyse images and hold conversations has revived these fears, partly because, for the first time, the technology appears to threaten professional and office jobs as well as manual ones.

Economists generally find it more useful to think about tasks than about whole occupations. Most jobs consist of many different tasks, and only some of these can be performed by machines. Historically, the tasks most easily automated have been routine ones that follow clear and predictable rules, such as assembling identical parts on a production line, sorting mail or entering figures into a spreadsheet. By contrast, tasks that demand physical flexibility in unpredictable settings, social understanding or creativity have proved much harder to automate. A robot can weld a car door with near-perfect accuracy, yet it still struggles to tidy an unfamiliar room or to comfort a frightened patient.

This distinction helps to explain why forecasts of job losses have varied so widely. One widely discussed early study, which assessed whole occupations, concluded that almost half of all jobs in the United States faced a high risk of automation within one or two decades. Later research that examined the individual tasks within each job produced far lower estimates, typically suggesting that around one job in ten was at high risk, although a much larger share would see some of their tasks change significantly. Generative AI has complicated the picture further, since it can carry out non-routine work such as drafting reports or writing computer code.

Historical evidence suggests that automation more often transforms jobs than eliminates them. When automated teller machines spread across American banks in the 1980s and 1990s, many observers expected the number of human bank tellers to collapse. Instead, because each branch now needed fewer staff, banks found it cheaper to open new branches, and teller employment remained broadly stable for many years. The nature of the work changed, however: tellers spent less time counting cash and more time advising customers and selling financial products. Technology also creates entirely new occupations. Many of today's common job titles, from software developer to social media manager, would have meant nothing to workers fifty years ago.

None of this means that the transition is painless. The gains from automation tend to be unevenly distributed. In many advanced economies, employment has grown in well-paid professional jobs and in low-paid service jobs, while middle-skill jobs in factories and offices have declined, a pattern known as job polarisation. Workers who lose such jobs frequently find new employment only at lower wages, and older workers in particular may never fully recover their previous earnings. Moreover, new jobs are often created in different places from those where old ones disappear, leaving some industrial regions in long-term decline.

For these reasons, most researchers argue that the central policy challenge is not to stop automation but to help workers move between tasks and jobs. Reskilling, which means training workers for substantially different roles, is the most frequently proposed response. Singapore, for example, gives adult citizens credits that can be spent on approved training courses, while Denmark combines relatively easy hiring and firing with generous unemployment benefits and active help in finding new work. Such programmes are not cheap, and their results vary. Training appears to work best when it is closely linked to jobs that employers actually need to fill, and when workers receive income support while they learn.

Other proposals are more controversial. Some commentators have suggested a tax on robots, both to slow the pace of automation and to fund support for displaced workers. Critics reply that a robot would be hard to define for tax purposes and that such a tax could discourage investment that raises productivity. A universal basic income, a regular payment to every citizen regardless of employment, has also been proposed. Small trials in several countries have produced mixed results, and the cost of a national scheme would be very high.

The future of work, then, will be shaped less by technology itself than by the choices societies make in response to it. Automation will probably continue to raise productivity and to create new kinds of employment, but whether its benefits are widely shared depends on education systems, labour-market institutions and public policy. In my view, the greater danger is not that machines will take all the jobs, but that governments will act too slowly to support the people whose jobs change.

questions.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Artificial intelligence will soon replace most professional and office workers.
Robots now outperform humans at repetitive work but not at creative work.
Retraining schemes in Singapore and Denmark have ended unemployment there.
Automation changes work more than it destroys it, but workers need support.
questions.explain: บทความชี้ว่า “automation more often transforms jobs than eliminates them” (¶4) แต่การเปลี่ยนผ่านสร้างความเดือดร้อน (¶5) จึงต้องมีนโยบายช่วยแรงงาน (¶6–8) ตัวเลือก D จึงครอบคลุมที่สุด ตัวเลือก B เป็นเพียงเนื้อหาของ ¶2 ส่วน A ขัดกับ ¶8 ที่ว่าอันตรายไม่ใช่การที่เครื่องจักรจะแย่งงานทั้งหมด

questions.q: According to paragraph 1, why do many people find recent artificial intelligence especially worrying?
options: It has already caused large numbers of people to lose their jobs.
It seems to threaten office jobs, not only manual ones.
It costs less than the industrial robots used in factories.
It was developed much more quickly than earlier technologies.
questions.explain: ¶1: “for the first time, the technology appears to threaten professional and office jobs as well as manual ones” จึงตอบ B ตัวเลือก A ผิดเพราะบทความพูดถึง 'ความกลัว' ว่าจะตกงาน ไม่ได้บอกว่ามีคนตกงานจำนวนมากแล้ว ส่วน C และ D ไม่มีกล่าวไว้

questions.q: The word 'revived' in paragraph 1 is closest in meaning to
options: brought back
calmed
caused for the first time
proved wrong
questions.explain: ¶1: AI “has revived these fears” โดย these fears คือคำเตือนที่มีมาตั้งแต่ยุคเครื่องทอผ้าและหุ่นยนต์อุตสาหกรรม revived จึงหมายถึงทำให้กลับมาอีกครั้ง (brought back) ตัวเลือก C เป็นกับดัก เพราะความกลัวนี้มีอยู่ก่อนแล้ว ไม่ได้เกิดขึ้นเป็นครั้งแรก

questions.q: What is paragraph 2 mainly about?
options: the history of robots in car factories
why office workers are afraid of losing their jobs
which tasks are easy or hard to automate
how forecasts of job losses are made
questions.explain: ¶2 เปรียบเทียบงาน routine ที่ “most easily automated” กับงานที่ต้องใช้ความยืดหยุ่น ความเข้าใจทางสังคม หรือความคิดสร้างสรรค์ซึ่ง “much harder to automate” จึงตอบ C ตัวเลือก A ผิดเพราะการเชื่อมประตูรถเป็นเพียงตัวอย่างประกอบ ส่วน D เป็นหัวข้อของ ¶3

questions.q: What does 'it' in paragraph 3 refer to?
options: this distinction
generative AI
the picture
computer code
questions.explain: ¶3: “Generative AI has complicated the picture further, since it can carry out non-routine work such as drafting reports or writing computer code.” สิ่งที่ร่างรายงานและเขียนโค้ดได้คือ generative AI ตัวเลือก C ผิดเพราะ the picture (ภาพรวมของการคาดการณ์) ไม่สามารถทำงานใด ๆ ได้

questions.q: It can be inferred from paragraph 3 that the early study produced a higher estimate mainly because it
options: focused only on jobs in factories
was carried out before computers were common
included the effects of generative AI
did not examine the tasks within each job
questions.explain: ¶3 ระบุว่างานศึกษาแรก “assessed whole occupations” ส่วนงานวิจัยภายหลังที่ “examined the individual tasks within each job” ได้ตัวเลขต่ำกว่ามาก จึงอนุมานได้ว่าตัวเลขสูงเพราะไม่ได้แยกพิจารณางานย่อย ตัวเลือก C ผิดเพราะ generative AI ถูกกล่าวถึงว่าเป็นปัจจัยที่เข้ามาภายหลัง

questions.q: Why does the author mention automated teller machines in paragraph 4?
options: to show that a job can change without disappearing
to explain why banks closed so many of their branches
to argue that bank tellers were paid too little
to give an example of a job created by technology
questions.explain: ตัวอย่างตู้ ATM สนับสนุนประโยคแรกของ ¶4 ว่า “automation more often transforms jobs than eliminates them” พนักงานธนาคารไม่ได้หายไป แต่ลักษณะงานเปลี่ยน จึงตอบ A ตัวเลือก B ตรงข้ามกับข้อความที่ว่าธนาคาร “open new branches” ส่วน D หมายถึงอาชีพใหม่ซึ่งเป็นอีกประเด็นในตอนท้ายย่อหน้า

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT mentioned in paragraph 5 as a problem linked to automation?
options: lower wages for workers who find new jobs
older workers never regaining their past earnings
longer hours for workers who keep their jobs
the long-term decline of some industrial regions
questions.explain: ¶5 กล่าวถึงค่าจ้างที่ต่ำลง (“only at lower wages”), แรงงานสูงวัยที่ “may never fully recover their previous earnings” และภูมิภาคอุตสาหกรรมที่ “in long-term decline” แต่ไม่ได้พูดถึงชั่วโมงทำงานที่ยาวขึ้นเลย จึงตอบ C

questions.q: According to paragraph 6, training appears to work best when
options: it is paid for entirely by the workers themselves
it is linked to jobs that employers need to fill
it replaces unemployment benefits completely
it is offered only to younger workers
questions.explain: ¶6: “Training appears to work best when it is closely linked to jobs that employers actually need to fill, and when workers receive income support while they learn.” จึงตอบ B ตัวเลือก C ขัดกับเงื่อนไขข้อที่สองที่ว่าผู้เรียนควรได้รับการสนับสนุนด้านรายได้ ไม่ใช่ตัดสวัสดิการออก

questions.q: The word 'displaced' in paragraph 7 is closest in meaning to
options: retired
relocated
skilled
jobless
questions.explain: ¶7: “to fund support for displaced workers” ในบริบทของภาษีหุ่นยนต์ displaced workers คือแรงงานที่ถูกเครื่องจักรแทนที่จนตกงาน จึงตรงกับ jobless ตัวเลือก B (relocated) เป็นกับดัก เพราะ displaced ในบริบทอื่นอาจหมายถึงการถูกย้ายออกจากที่อยู่ แต่ที่นี่ไม่ได้พูดถึงการย้ายถิ่น

questions.q: It can be inferred from paragraph 7 that the author regards the two proposals discussed there as
options: ideas with serious practical problems
the policies most economists now support
cheaper alternatives to reskilling
proven ways of reducing unemployment
questions.explain: ¶7 เปิดด้วย “Other proposals are more controversial.” แล้วชี้ปัญหาของทั้งสองแนวคิด เช่น นิยามหุ่นยนต์ได้ยาก และ “the cost of a national scheme would be very high” จึงอนุมานได้ว่าผู้เขียนมองว่ามีอุปสรรคในทางปฏิบัติมาก ตัวเลือก D ผิดเพราะการทดลองให้ผล “mixed results”

questions.q: Which of the following is an opinion rather than a fact?
options: Automated teller machines spread across American banks in the 1980s.
Singapore gives adult citizens credits for approved training courses.
The greater danger is that governments will act too slowly.
Small trials of regular unconditional payments have produced mixed results.
questions.explain: ¶8: “In my view, the greater danger is not that machines will take all the jobs, but that governments will act too slowly…” วลี In my view แสดงว่าเป็นความเห็นของผู้เขียน ส่วน A, B และ D เป็นข้อเท็จจริงที่ตรวจสอบได้จาก ¶4, ¶6 และ ¶7

questions.q: In paragraph 2, which word describes tasks such as sorting mail or entering figures into a spreadsheet? (Answer in ONE WORD from the passage.)
questions.explain: ¶2: “the tasks most easily automated have been routine ones that follow clear and predictable rules, such as assembling identical parts on a production line, sorting mail or entering figures into a spreadsheet” คำตอบคือ routine (งานที่ทำซ้ำตามกฎชัดเจน) ซึ่งเป็นงานที่เครื่องจักรทำแทนได้ง่ายที่สุด

questions.q: Apart from selling financial products, what did bank tellers spend more time doing after cash machines spread? (Answer in NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS from the passage.)
questions.explain: ¶4: “tellers spent less time counting cash and more time advising customers and selling financial products” คำตอบคือ advising customers ส่วน counting cash เป็นงานที่ 'ลดลง' จึงไม่ใช่คำตอบ

questions.q: What name is given to the pattern in which middle-skill jobs decline while well-paid and low-paid jobs grow? (Answer in NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS from the passage.)
questions.explain: ¶5: “while middle-skill jobs in factories and offices have declined, a pattern known as job polarisation” คำตอบคือ job polarisation หมายถึงตลาดแรงงานที่แยกเป็นสองขั้ว คืองานรายได้สูงและงานรายได้ต่ำ

questions.q: Which term does the author use for training workers for substantially different roles? (Answer in ONE WORD from the passage.)
questions.explain: ¶6: “Reskilling, which means training workers for substantially different roles, is the most frequently proposed response.” คำตอบคือ reskilling ซึ่งต่างจากการฝึกเพิ่มทักษะในงานเดิม

questions.q: What is the name of the proposed regular payment to every citizen regardless of employment? (Answer in NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS from the passage.)
questions.explain: ¶7: “A universal basic income, a regular payment to every citizen regardless of employment, has also been proposed.” คำตอบคือ universal basic income (รายได้พื้นฐานถ้วนหน้า) ไม่ใช่ robot tax ซึ่งเป็นข้อเสนออีกข้อในย่อหน้าเดียวกัน
